content: The Western Larch, scientifically known as Larix occidentalis, is a species of larch tree native to the mountainous regions of western North America. Its natural range includes southeastern British Columbia and southwestern Alberta in Canada, as well as eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, northern Idaho, and western Montana in the United States. This tree can grow to a diameter of up to 5 meters. Its crown is narrow and conical in shape, with main branches that are either level or slightly upswept, while the side branches often droop. The shoots of the Western Larch are dimorphic, meaning they exhibit two distinct forms. The long shoots, which typically measure 10–50 cm in length, bear several buds, whereas the short shoots are only 1–2 mm long and have a single bud. The leaves of the Western Larch are needle-like, light green in color, and measure 2–5 cm in length. They are very slender and turn a bright yellow in the fall before shedding, leaving the pale orange-brown shoots bare until the following spring. The cones of the tree are ovoid-cylindrical, measuring 2–5 cm in length, and consist of 40–80 seed scales. Each scale has a protruding bract that is 4–8 mm long. Immature cones are red, but they turn brown as they mature, with the scales opening flat or reflexed to release seeds approximately 4–6 months after pollination. Old cones often remain on the tree for many years, eventually turning a dull gray-black. The Western Larch thrives at altitudes ranging from 500 to 2,400 meters and is highly tolerant of cold temperatures, capable of surviving winter conditions as low as −50°C. However, it requires well-drained soils and avoids waterlogged areas. The seeds of the tree serve as an important food source for certain bird species, including the Pine Siskin, Common Redpoll, and White-winged Crossbill. Uses The wood of the Western Larch is tough, durable, and flexible when cut into thin strips. It is particularly valued in yacht building, but the wood used for this purpose must be free of knots, which can only be obtained from older trees that were pruned in their youth to remove side branches. Small larch poles are commonly used for rustic fencing. Additionally, the Western Larch is a source of Venice turpentine. In the Pacific Northwest, the wood is highly prized as firewood and is often referred to as Tamarack, although it is a different species from the Tamarack Larch. When burned, the wood emits a sweet fragrance and produces a distinctive popping sound. Indigenous peoples historically chewed gum derived from the tree and consumed its cambium and sap.
